migrationNotes: Spine: watch one meadow of blue and gold beetles. Count the shares, see what the birds do to them, name the process, change the meadow to reverse it, and finish on what else could move a share.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-natural-selection-hook and -count-vs-share. The hook's 8 beetles are worked in the screen on the birds; the comparison of counts and shares is made in the first screen. Green beetles became blue and gold ones so that the figure's blue and gold variants match the story; the key of -env-b (20) is unchanged.

lesson.title: A population changes over generations

lead.text: Start by counting. At the beginning there are 16 blue beetles and 24 gold ones, 40 in all. A group of one kind of living thing in one place is a population, and the different forms within it, such as blue and gold, are variants. To say how common a variant is, we use its frequency, which is its count divided by the size of the whole population, usually written as a percentage.

Here the blue beetles have a frequency of 16 ÷ 40 = 0.4, which is 40%, and the gold beetles have 24 ÷ 40 = 60%. Frequency is useful because it ignores the size of the group. A meadow with twice as many beetles, 32 blue and 48 gold, has the same frequencies, since 32 ÷ 80 = 40%. A count says how many beetles there are. A frequency says what share of the population they make.
Divide the count of the variant by the size of the whole group.

steps.headline: What the birds did to the shares

lead.text: Back to the meadow. The birds eat half of the 16 blue beetles, which leaves 8. The 24 gold beetles are untouched. The meadow now holds 8 + 24 = 32 beetles. The blue frequency has changed to 8 ÷ 32 = 25%, down from 40% before.

The size of a change in frequency is the difference between the two percentages. A frequency is already a percentage, so we call that difference percentage points: 40% − 25% = 15 percentage points. The blue frequency fell by 15 points. Saying points avoids a muddle between a fall of 15 points and a fall of 15 percent of 40, which would be only 6 points.

afterFigure.text: The survivors are the parents of the next generation. Suppose each beetle leaves two offspring and colour passes from parent to young. Then 8 blue beetles leave 16 blue young and 24 gold beetles leave 48 gold young. The new generation has 64 beetles, and the blue frequency is 16 ÷ 64 = 25%. What the birds changed in one season has been carried into the next generation.

lead.text: Work out each frequency first, then find the difference between them.

What happened in the meadow has a name. In any population the individuals differ. Some differences are heritable, which means they pass from parents to offspring. The beetles' colour is one, since blue parents tend to have blue young. Other differences, such as a scratch on a wing, are not heritable, because the young are born without them.

Natural selection happens when the carriers of one heritable variant leave more offspring than the carriers of another, in the environment where they live. The variant that does better then makes up a bigger share of each new generation, and its frequency rises generation after generation. Here the birds favoured the gold beetles, which were more likely to survive and breed.
Nobody decides this. No beetle changes colour to hide, and no bird intends to alter the meadow. The shift happens because some variants leave more offspring than others.
Think about what is changing the shares of the variants in the meadow.

Whether a variant helps depends on where it lives. Blue is a handicap on dry golden grass, because the birds spot it. Move the beetles to a woodland floor carpeted in bluebells, and it is the gold beetles that stand out. The same variants face the same birds and the result is the opposite one.

In the figure the same mixed group of 40 beetles, 20 blue and 20 gold, is placed in two environments. In environment A, the bluebell wood, the blue beetles do well and their frequency rises from 50% to 70%. In environment B, the golden meadow, the blue beetles do badly and their frequency falls to 30%. The beetles are the same in both places. Only the environment differs.

afterFigure.text: So a trait is neither good nor bad by itself. A variant that rises in one environment can fall in another, and when an environment changes, the same variant can go from an advantage to a handicap.

lead.text: In a golden meadow the blue beetles do badly, as in environment B.

A change in frequency shows that something happened. It does not show that selection did it. Chance alone can change the shares, especially in a small population. Take 10 beetles, 5 blue and 5 gold, and suppose a storm kills 6 of them without regard to colour. By bad luck 4 of the 6 are gold and 2 are blue. The 4 survivors are 3 blue and 1 gold, so the blue frequency has risen from 5 ÷ 10 = 50% to 3 ÷ 4 = 75%. That is a rise of 25 points with no advantage behind it.

Migration can do the same thing. If 40 gold beetles fly in to a meadow of 20 blue and 20 gold, the blue frequency falls from 50% to 20 ÷ 80 = 25%, whatever the birds do. To credit natural selection you need evidence that the variants really differ in the offspring they leave, and a shift in the shares cannot supply that on its own.
A variant has become more common in a small population.

lesson.orientation: Connect heritable variation and reproductive success without confusing change with proof of cause.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A meadow of dry golden grass is home to 40 beetles. Sixteen are bright blue and 24 are gold. The gold ones are hard to see against the grass, while the blue ones show up from the air, and a flock of birds that hunt by sight has found the meadow.

Before the beetles have a chance to breed, the birds eat half of the blue beetles and none of the gold, which they overlook. The beetles that survive will mate and lay eggs, and their young will grow up in the same meadow. Colour runs in families, so blue parents tend to have blue young and gold parents tend to have gold young.

The last lesson explained where new versions of a trait come from. This lesson asks what happens to them afterwards. It follows the beetles through one season and then a generation, counting how many of each colour there are and what share of the meadow each makes up, and it asks what that tells us and what it leaves open.

intro.promise: By the end you'll calculate how a variant's share of a population changes, and say what natural selection does and does not show.

recap.keyIdea: Heritable variants that leave more offspring become more common, and which variants do so depends on the environment. A frequency shift alone does not prove selection.

blocks.text: You turned beetle counts into frequencies and measured a fall of 15 percentage points and a rise of 30. You saw the same variant rise in one environment and fall in another, and you found that chance or migration can move a frequency without selection.

recap.nextHook: A population changes with what surrounds it: its food, its enemies and the weather. The next lesson widens the view from one species to a whole pond and follows who eats whom.

questions.prompt: 10 of 40 organisms carry the blue variant. What percentage is blue?
hints: Use the blue count divided by the total.
The total is the blue and the other colour together.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 25%. A frequency is the variant's count divided by the whole population.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Divide it by the whole population and convert to a percentage.
That is the share that is not blue.

questions.prompt: Heritable variants consistently leave different numbers of reproducing descendants. Name the evolutionary process described.
hints: The difference is consistent, unlike random sampling.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Natural selection changes frequencies through differences in reproductive success associated with heritable traits.

questions.onCorrect: Natural selection. Heritable differences in offspring numbers shift the frequencies.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutation creates new variants. This is the sorting of variants that already exist.
The question says the difference is consistent and tied to the variant, which is not chance.

questions.prompt: Blue organisms increase from 15 of 50 to 30 of 50. By how many percentage points does the blue frequency rise?
hints: Calculate each frequency using the total of 50.
Convert each fraction to a percentage.
Subtract the earlier percentage from the later one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The frequency rises from 30% to 60%, a 30-point increase.

questions.onCorrect: 30 points. Work out both frequencies, then subtract.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise in count. The question asks for the rise in frequency.
That is the later frequency, not the rise.

questions.prompt: A small population's variant frequency changes. Is selection the only possible cause?
hints: A pattern can have more than one cause.

acceptedIdeas: No, chance and migration can also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Several evolutionary processes can change frequency; causal evidence is needed.

choices.label: Yes, every frequency shift proves selection
No, chance and migration can also matter

questions.onCorrect: No. Chance and migration also shift frequencies, so a shift alone does not show selection.

misconceptions.feedback: A shift only shows that a frequency changed. It does not say why.
Populations change all the time, which is why the question matters.

questions.prompt: A once-useful trait becomes disadvantageous after a habitat change. Is this compatible with natural selection?
hints: Fitness depends on context.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, reproductive advantage depends on the environment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selection depends on how traits affect reproduction in the current environment.

choices.label: No, useful traits are always useful
Only if the organism chooses it
Yes, reproductive advantage depends on the environment

questions.onCorrect: Yes. A trait's advantage depends on the environment, so a new habitat can reverse it.

misconceptions.feedback: Usefulness depends on the environment, so a trait can stop helping.
Organisms do not choose the effect of their traits. The environment sets it.

questions.prompt: A later population has 18 blue and 42 gold organisms. What percentage is blue?
hints: Find the total population.
Divide the blue count by the total.
Convert the result to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 30%. Blue is 18 of 60, so its share is a little under a third.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the blue count. Divide it by the whole population.
That is the share that is gold.

questions.prompt: Natural selection acts only on differences that pass from parents to offspring. What word describes such differences?
hints: The word comes from inherit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Heritable differences can be passed on, so selection can change their frequency.

questions.onCorrect: Heritable. A difference that is not passed on cannot change the next generation.

misconceptions.feedback: Traits gained during a lifetime are not passed on in the way selection needs.

questions.prompt: How many green beetles are left?
hints: Only the green beetles are eaten.
The birds eat half of them.
Halve the number of green beetles.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Half of 16 is 8, so 8 green beetles remain.

questions.onCorrect: 8. One colour is removed faster than the other, so the colours' shares of the population will shift.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many green beetles there were before the birds ate any.
That takes half of the whole meadow. The birds ate only half of the green beetles.

questions.prompt: Why compare percentages instead of counts when the population size changes?
hints: What happens to a count if the population doubles?

acceptedIdeas: A count changes with the size of the population, but a frequency does not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A frequency is a share of the whole, so it can be compared between populations of different sizes.

choices.label: A count changes with the size of the population, but a frequency does not
Percentages are always larger than counts

questions.onCorrect: A share of the whole stays comparable when the population size changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Size has nothing to do with which number is larger. The point is what each one measures.
Counts can be added. The problem is comparing populations of different sizes.

questions.prompt: In a golden meadow, blue beetles fall from 20 of 40 to 8 of 40. What percentage of the beetles is blue afterwards?
hints: Use the blue count divided by the total.
The total is still the same number of beetles.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 20%. In this environment blue does worse, so its share falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count. Convert it into a share of the total.
That is the share that is not blue.
